summary: Describes how a PIM multicast tree that crosses an MPLS network can be carried over multipoint LDP label switched paths. When a PIM Join arrives at the MPLS edge, information in it is used to set up the multipoint LSP, with no separate provisioning.

eli5.summary: A group message must cross a tunnel city. When someone asks to join, the tunnel quietly builds a branch for them, using the request itself as the plan.

questions: how does pim signal mpls multicast lsps
how does pim work over mpls
subtitle: How a PIM multicast tree can cross an MPLS network by hiding its source and group inside the mLDP label request itself.

tldr.problem: mLDP can build multipoint label switched paths, but it has no rule for tying a particular end-user multicast stream to a particular path.
tldr.mechanism: The multicast source and group (or RP and group) are carried in the opaque value field of the mLDP FEC element, so the far edge of the MPLS network can read them back out and continue the multicast tree with PIM.
tldr.outcome: A multicast tree becomes IP sub-trees spliced together by a multipoint LSP, with one LSP per tree. The RFC was later updated by RFC 7438.

today: RFC 6826 is a Proposed Standard that was updated by RFC 7438. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: The Problem and the Idea
sections.content:
Multipoint LDP (mLDP, from RFC 6388) can create point-to-multipoint (P2MP) and multipoint-to-multipoint (MP2MP) label switched paths. They are typically used to carry end-user multicast packets. But mLDP itself gives no rules for deciding which multicast packets belong on which LSP. Other documents, such as RFC 6513, solve this with out-of-band signaling, for example PIM and BGP.

This RFC describes in-band signaling instead. The information that maps an LSP to its multicast packets travels in the opaque value field of an mLDP FEC (Forwarding Equivalence Class) element. When a tree enters the MPLS network, its (S,G) or (*,G) state goes into that field. When the tree leaves the MPLS network, the information is pulled back out and used to build IP multicast state, and PIM messages can be sent outside the MPLS domain.

PIM control messages are sent periodically, but the mLDP messages are not. Each IP multicast tree maps one-to-one to a P2MP or MP2MP LSP, so an operator should expect as many LSPs as there are trees, and should keep the state within the scaling limits of PIM and mLDP.
sections.eli5: Normally the tunnel does not know which group messages belong in which lane. Here, the request to join writes the answer on the lane itself.

sections.title: How In-Band Signaling Works
sections.content:
The RFC's example topology is a source or RP, then IP multicast router A, MPLS routers U, C and D, IP multicast router B, and a receiver. Router D must build an IP multicast tree because of an event such as a PIM Join, an MSDP Source Announcement, a BGP Source Active auto-discovery route or RP discovery. If D finds that the tree must cross the MPLS network to reach LSR U (for example, U is the BGP next hop toward the source), D may set up a P2MP or MP2MP LSP rooted at U.

To do this, D encodes a P2MP or MP2MP FEC element. The Root Node Address is the address of U, and the source and group go into the opaque value. D MUST NOT use an opaque value type unless it knows, through provisioning or other means outside this document, that U supports the root node procedures for that type.

An LSR that receives a label mapping or withdraw with one of these opaque types, and is not the root, follows the ordinary RFC 6388 procedures. The root extracts the source and group and hands them to its multicast code. On a label mapping, the code adds the downstream LDP neighbor to the olist of the matching (S,G) or (*,G) state, creating it if needed. On a withdraw, it removes that neighbor. After that, normal PIM processing happens.

If the root does not recognize the opaque value type, the LSP is still established, but the root sends no multicast data on it.
sections.eli5: The last router before the tunnel writes who is sending and which group on the lane request. The router at the start of the lane reads it and hands it to the group-messaging software.

sections.title: Which Trees Are Covered
sections.content:
Shared trees used by PIM-SM in the ASM service model are out of scope. Nothing stops them crossing an MPLS core, but individual sources cannot be pruned from a shared tree without an extra out-of-band protocol such as PIM or BGP.

Source trees are covered. They can be created by PIM in SSM mode (RFC 4607) or ASM mode (RFC 4601). For ASM, this document gives no way to build a sparse-mode shared tree across MPLS, so some other means of discovering active sources is needed, such as MSDP or BGP Source Active auto-discovery routes. That discovery is outside the document, so it does not specify everything needed for the ASM service model with in-band signaling.

Also out of scope are source or RP addresses reachable in a VPN context, and groups running in PIM Dense-Mode.
sections.eli5: The tunnel only handles some kinds of group messages. Messages that need extra rules about who to ignore are left for other documents.

sections.title: Bidirectional Trees
sections.content:
A bidirectional tree (RFC 5015) transported this way MUST use an MP2MP LSP. It has no specific source address. The group address, subnet mask and RP matter for forwarding. The RP selects the ingress LSR and the root of the LSP, and the RFC assumes the RP is statically defined; discovering RP-to-group mappings dynamically is not covered.

There are two kinds of bidirectional state: group-specific state, usually created by a PIM Join with a subnet mask of 32 for IPv4 and 128 for IPv6, and RP state, usually created by static RP mapping with a variable mask. RP state builds a tree to the RP and is used for sender-only branches. Each state gets its own MP2MP LSP, and PIM merges the two at the root LSR, treating each LSP as a PIM-enabled interface.

Packets from a sender-only branch travel on an MP2MP LSP. Other sender-only branches receive them and drop them because they have no receivers. If that is undesirable, some other transport to the root is needed, such as a multipoint-to-point LSP.
sections.eli5: When everyone in a group can both send and listen, the tunnel needs a two-way lane. Two lanes get joined together at the meeting point.

sections.title: The Transit TLV Encodings
sections.content:
Four new opaque value types, called Transit TLVs, carry the tree identity. Each starts with a one-octet Type and a two-octet Length, as drawn in the RFC.

  • Transit IPv4 Source (Type 3): Length 8, then a 4-octet source and a 4-octet group.
  • Transit IPv6 Source (Type 4): Length 32, then a 16-octet source and a 16-octet group.
  • Transit IPv4 Bidir (Type 5): Length 9, then a 1-octet Mask Len (maximum 32), a 4-octet RP address and a 4-octet group.
  • Transit IPv6 Bidir (Type 6): Length 33, then a 1-octet Mask Len (maximum 128), a 16-octet RP address and a 16-octet group.

Mask Len is the number of contiguous one bits, left-justified, used as a mask.
sections.eli5: There are four kinds of label for the request, one for each mix of address size and group type. Each says who or where the group is.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds nothing new here. The same security considerations apply as for the base LDP specification, described in RFC 5036.
sections.eli5: The tunnel uses the same locks it already had. No new locks are added.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content: IANA allocated four values from the LDP MP Opaque Value Element basic type registry: Transit IPv4 Source TLV type 3, Transit IPv6 Source TLV type 4, Transit IPv4 Bidir TLV type 5 and Transit IPv6 Bidir TLV type 6.
sections.eli5: The number-keeper gave each of the four labels its own number so nobody mixes them up.

items.label: Transit IPv4 Source
items.desc: Length 8: IPv4 source and group, 4 octets each.

items.label: Transit IPv6 Source
items.desc: Length 32: IPv6 source and group, 16 octets each.

items.label: Transit IPv4 Bidir
items.desc: Length 9: mask length, IPv4 RP and group.

items.label: Transit IPv6 Bidir
items.desc: Length 33: mask length, IPv6 RP and group.
